content: Pharyngitis, commonly referred to as a sore throat, is characterized by inflammation of the pharynx, often presenting with pain, fever, and redness or swelling of the throat. In some cases, additional findings such as exudates, vesicles, or ulcerations may be observed. This condition is a frequent reason for outpatient medical visits, particularly in pediatric populations, accounting for over seven million visits annually. The majority of pharyngitis cases are caused by infectious agents, with viral infections being the most common etiology. However, bacterial causes, such as Group A Streptococcus (GAS), are responsible for more severe cases and can lead to complications like rheumatic fever, deep space abscesses, and toxic shock syndrome. While most cases of pharyngitis are acute, a small percentage may become recurrent or chronic. Chronic pharyngitis may be associated with non-infectious causes, such as laryngopharyngeal reflux disease or periodic fever, aphthous ulcers, pharyngitis, and adenitis (PFAPA) syndrome. Management of pharyngitis includes both medical and surgical options. Antibiotics are the first-line treatment for bacterial pharyngitis, particularly GAS. Surgical intervention, such as adenotonsillectomy, may be indicated in certain cases, especially for recurrent infections. Adenotonsillectomy has been shown to reduce disease burden and improve quality of life. Historically, pharyngitis was first described in 1879 by R.L. Bowles, M.D., and further elaborated upon in 1885 by David Newman, M.D., who detailed its pathology, symptoms, and treatment. The importance of bacteriological testing in uncertain cases was recognized in 1910, and by 1931, chronic nasopharyngitis was linked to conditions like influenza, whooping cough, and measles. The pathophysiology of pharyngitis involves the pharynx as a primary site of infection for many pathogens, including viruses and bacteria. Transmission typically occurs via direct contact or respiratory droplets. Viral pharyngitis is often self-limiting, but bacterial pharyngitis, particularly due to GAS, requires prompt diagnosis and treatment to prevent complications. Pharyngitis can be caused by infectious agents (viruses, bacteria, fungi) or non-infectious factors such as gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) or extra-esophageal reflux (EER). It is classified based on duration as either acute or chronic. The primary goal in evaluating pharyngitis is to identify treatable causes, such as GAS, to prevent complications like acute rheumatic fever and post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. Differential diagnoses include conditions that mimic sore throat, such as oral thrush, infectious mononucleosis, epiglottitis, and peritonsillar abscess. Pharyngitis is highly prevalent, with over 10 million outpatient visits annually in the United States. Viral infections account for 25–45% of cases, while GAS is the most common bacterial cause, responsible for 15–30% of cases in children and 5–10% in adults. The incidence of pharyngitis peaks in late winter and early spring. Risk factors include close contact with infected individuals, overcrowding, smoking, frequent sinus infections, and immunocompromised states. Acute pharyngitis typically presents with sore throat, fever, and pharyngeal inflammation. Most cases are benign and self-limiting, but a small percentage may progress to chronic disease. Diagnosis involves identifying treatable causes, particularly GAS, to prevent complications. Clinical features of GAS pharyngitis include sudden onset of sore throat, tonsillar or pharyngeal exudates, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and fever. Viral pharyngitis may present with conjunctivitis, cough, oral ulcers, and diarrhea. Rapid antigen detection tests (RADTs) are commonly used to diagnose GAS, with throat cultures serving as a confirmatory test in children when RADTs are negative. In adults, GAS accounts for only 5–15% of pharyngitis cases. The risk of complications like acute rheumatic fever is extremely low in this population, so routine throat cultures are not necessary for adults with negative RADTs. Treatment of pharyngitis caused by GAS involves a 10-day course of penicillin or amoxicillin for non-allergic individuals. Alternatives for penicillin-allergic patients include first-generation cephalosporins, clindamycin, clarithromycin, or a 5-day course of azithromycin. Adjunctive therapies, such as NSAIDs, acetaminophen, or corticosteroids, may help alleviate symptoms. Tonsillectomy may be considered for patients with recurrent streptococcal infections. Prevention of complications, such as acute rheumatic fever and suppurative conditions like peritonsillar abscess, relies on accurate diagnosis and appropriate antibiotic therapy for GAS pharyngitis.
